title: Goroutines
summary: A **goroutine** is a lightweight thread of execution managed by the Go runtime — start one by writing `go` in front of any function call. They are so cheap that a single program can run hundreds of thousands of them, which is what makes Go's concurrency model so powerful.

subtopics.title: The go keyword
subtopics.explanation: Writing `go f(x)` evaluates f and x immediately, then schedules the call to run concurrently. Control returns to the caller right away — it does NOT wait for f to finish.
subtopics.example: go process(req) // runs in the background

subtopics.title: The GMP scheduler
subtopics.explanation: The runtime multiplexes Goroutines (G) onto logical Processors (P, count = GOMAXPROCS) which are bound to OS threads (M). When a goroutine blocks, the scheduler parks it and runs another on the same thread, so threads stay busy.
subtopics.example: runtime.GOMAXPROCS(4) // up to 4 goroutines running in parallel

subtopics.title: Waiting with sync.WaitGroup
subtopics.explanation: A WaitGroup is a counter: Add(n) before launching, Done() (deferred) inside each goroutine, and Wait() blocks until the counter hits zero. Add must happen before the goroutine can call Done.
subtopics.example: wg.Add(1); go func(){ defer wg.Done(); work() }(); wg.Wait()

subtopics.title: Concurrency vs parallelism
subtopics.explanation: Concurrency is structuring a program as independently-executing tasks; parallelism is running them at the same instant. Goroutines give you concurrency; multiple cores plus GOMAXPROCS>1 give you parallelism.

subtopics.title: Goroutine leaks
subtopics.explanation: A goroutine blocked forever (e.g. on a channel with no sender, or with no cancellation) never returns — a memory and resource leak. Always give every goroutine a clear exit path (return, channel close, or context cancellation).
subtopics.example: select { case <-ctx.Done(): return; case v := <-ch: use(v) }

foundations.overview: Putting `go` before a function call tells the Go runtime: 'run this in the background and keep going.' That single keyword launches a goroutine — a function that runs concurrently with everything else in the same address space. The runtime, not the operating system, decides when each goroutine runs, which is exactly why goroutines are so cheap that you can have hundreds of thousands of them.
foundations.formalDefinition: A goroutine is a function executing concurrently with other goroutines in the same address space, scheduled cooperatively by the Go runtime onto a small pool of OS threads.
foundations.whyItMatters: Goroutines are the foundation of every concurrent Go program — servers, pipelines, parallel workloads. They let you write concurrent code that reads almost like sequential code, and they are a guaranteed topic in any Go interview.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a kitchen: you (the main goroutine) call out orders and keep taking more, while cooks (goroutines) work in parallel. The head chef (the scheduler) assigns cooks to the few available stoves (OS threads), and a WaitGroup is the ticket rail you watch to know when every order is done.
foundations.runtimePerspective: Each goroutine starts with a tiny ~2KB stack that grows on demand. The runtime keeps run queues per processor (P), steals work between them to balance load, and since Go 1.14 can asynchronously preempt a goroutine stuck in a tight loop so it can't starve the others.
foundations.realWorldUsage: net/http runs each incoming request in its own goroutine; worker pools process jobs concurrently; pipelines connect stages with channels — all built on goroutines.
foundations.businessImpact: Because goroutines are so cheap, one Go service can handle thousands of concurrent requests on modest hardware, directly lowering infrastructure cost.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Goroutines + channels let teams express concurrency clearly, reducing the bug surface compared to manual thread and lock management.
foundations.performanceImpact: Cheap creation (~2KB vs ~1MB for OS threads) and efficient blocking-IO handling mean far higher concurrency per core; but unbounded goroutine creation can exhaust memory, so production code bounds it.
commonUseCases: One goroutine per request in HTTP servers
Worker pools consuming a jobs channel

commonMisconceptions.myth: A goroutine is an OS thread.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It is a runtime-managed coroutine multiplexed onto a small pool of OS threads (the GMP model).

commonMisconceptions.myth: Starting a goroutine runs it immediately.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It only becomes runnable; the scheduler decides when it runs — and if main() returns first, it may never run at all.
Past the point of useful parallelism, extra goroutines add scheduling and contention overhead.

config.intro: Launching and running a goroutine, step by step:

steps.name: Evaluate & enqueue
steps.detail: `go worker()` evaluates the function and its arguments now, then puts a new goroutine on a P's run queue.

steps.name: Caller continues
steps.detail: Control returns immediately to the calling goroutine — it does not wait.

steps.name: Scheduled to run
steps.detail: When a P/thread is free, the scheduler runs the goroutine, possibly in parallel with the caller.

steps.name: Block & switch
steps.detail: If it blocks on a channel or syscall, the scheduler parks it and runs another runnable goroutine on that thread.

steps.name: Finish
steps.detail: When it returns, its stack is reclaimed. If main() returns first, the whole program exits regardless.

interactiveExamples.title: Launch goroutines and wait for them
interactiveExamples.explanation: wg.Add(1) is called BEFORE `go`, and each worker defers wg.Done(). Passing i as an argument copies it per iteration, avoiding the loop-variable trap. wg.Wait() blocks main until all three finish.

code.expectedOutput:
worker 1 done
worker 2 done
worker 3 done
all workers done
(worker order may vary)

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: collect results over a channel
interactiveExamples.explanation: Goroutines can't return values directly. Here each goroutine sends its square on a buffered channel, and main collects them. Try changing n or the buffer size and reason about what happens.

code.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	n := 5
	results := make(chan int, n) // TODO: launch n goroutines that send i*i
	_ = results
	fmt.Println("fill in the goroutines")
}

checkpoints.prompt: What does this program most likely print?
checkpoints.explanation: main() prints its line and then returns immediately. When main returns the program exits, so the goroutine usually never gets scheduled. Without synchronization you can't rely on it running at all.

checkpoints.prompt: Where must wg.Add(1) be called to avoid a race with wg.Wait()?
options: Before the `go` statement that launches the goroutine
checkpoints.explanation: If Add runs inside the goroutine, Wait() in main might observe a zero counter before the goroutine is scheduled and return too early. Always Add before launching; Done() goes inside (deferred).

checkpoints.prompt: This pre-Go-1.22 code is meant to print a, b, c. What's the bug?
options: The closure captures the shared loop variable s
range can't be used with goroutines
checkpoints.explanation: Before Go 1.22 the loop variable s was shared across iterations, so all goroutines could print the last value ("c c c"). Fix it by passing s as an argument: go func(s string){...}(s), or shadow it with s := s.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the line so main waits for all goroutines to finish.
checkpoints.explanation: wg.Wait() blocks until the counter returns to zero. time.Sleep is a flaky guess at timing, Done() decrements (wrong here), and a WaitGroup can't be closed.

codeLab.title: Build a bounded worker pool
codeLab.instructions: Implement `Solve(nums, workers)` that sums nums using a pool of `workers` goroutines reading from a jobs channel, aggregating partial sums. The result must be deterministic.
hints: Put every number on a buffered jobs channel, then close it so `for range jobs` ends.
Each worker accumulates a partial sum and sends it once on a results channel.
Close the results channel in a separate goroutine after wg.Wait(), so the final `for range` terminates.

debuggingLab.title: The work never prints
debuggingLab.symptom: This program compiles and runs but prints nothing from the goroutine.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: There is no synchronization between main and the goroutine. main() returns immediately, and when main returns the program exits — the goroutine never gets a chance to run.
commonMistakes: Assuming `go` waits for the function to complete.
Using time.Sleep to 'fix' it (works by luck, not correctness).
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Make main wait for the goroutine using a sync.WaitGroup.

theory.question: What is a goroutine and how is it different from an OS thread?
theory.directAnswer: A goroutine is a lightweight, runtime-scheduled concurrent function started with the `go` keyword. Unlike an OS thread, it starts with a tiny ~2KB growable stack and is multiplexed by the Go runtime onto a small pool of OS threads, so you can run hundreds of thousands of them cheaply.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A function running concurrently in the same address space, managed by the Go scheduler rather than the OS.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To make concurrency cheap and easy so that idiomatic Go can express servers and pipelines without manual thread pools.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The runtime's GMP scheduler places goroutines (G) on processors (P) bound to threads (M), parking blocked goroutines and stealing work to keep cores busy.

theory.whyImportant: It's the foundation of Go concurrency and a near-guaranteed interview question.
theory.realWorldExample: An HTTP server runs each request in its own goroutine, so thousands of requests are handled concurrently on a handful of threads.

followUps.question: Why is a goroutine's stack only ~2KB?
followUps.answer: It starts small and grows/shrinks on demand, so creating many goroutines costs little memory compared to ~1MB OS-thread stacks.

followUps.question: What is GOMAXPROCS?
followUps.answer: The number of logical processors (P) that can run Go code simultaneously — effectively the max parallelism; it defaults to the number of CPUs.

theory.question: How do you wait for a set of goroutines to finish, and what's the Add/Done ordering rule?
theory.directAnswer: Use a sync.WaitGroup: call Add(n) before launching, defer Done() inside each goroutine, and Wait() to block until the counter reaches zero. Add must be called before the goroutine could run, otherwise Wait() may observe zero and return too early.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A counter-based synchronization primitive for awaiting goroutine completion.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Goroutines don't return values or join like threads; WaitGroup provides the join.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Add increments, Done decrements (usually deferred), Wait blocks until the count is zero.

theory.whyImportant: Coordinating completion correctly is a frequent source of subtle bugs and interview probing.
theory.realWorldExample: A handler fans out N downstream calls in goroutines and uses a WaitGroup to wait for all before responding.

followUps.question: What happens if you call Add inside the goroutine?
followUps.answer: A race: Wait() may run before Add, see zero, and return before the work is counted.

scenario.question: A long-running service's memory climbs steadily until it OOMs, and runtime.NumGoroutine() keeps increasing. What's happening and how do you fix it?
scenario.directAnswer: That's a goroutine leak: goroutines are blocked forever — typically on a channel send/receive with no peer, or with no cancellation path. Fix it by giving every goroutine a guaranteed exit: use context cancellation/timeouts, ensure channels get closed, and select on ctx.Done().

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Unbounded growth of goroutines that never return.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A goroutine blocked on I/O or a channel with no counterpart parks forever, holding its stack.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: NumGoroutine() rising monotonically is the tell; a goroutine pprof profile shows where they're stuck.

scenario.whyImportant: Goroutine leaks are one of the most common Go production incidents.
scenario.realWorldExample: A request spawns a goroutine that writes to an unbuffered channel, but the reader returns early on error, leaving the writer blocked forever.

followUps.question: How would you confirm the leak's location?
followUps.answer: Pull the goroutine profile from /debug/pprof/goroutine and look for many goroutines stuck on the same channel/select line.

coding.question: Run N independent tasks concurrently and return their results in order. Implement `func RunAll(tasks []func() int) []int`.
coding.thoughtProcess: Each task is independent, so run each in its own goroutine. To preserve order, give each goroutine the index and write into a pre-sized results slice at that index (no shared-slot races since indices are distinct). Use a WaitGroup to wait for all.
coding.lineByLine: res is sized up front so each goroutine writes a distinct index — distinct indices mean no overlapping memory, so no mutex is needed. We pass idx and fn as arguments to avoid the loop-variable capture bug. wg.Wait() blocks until every task has written its slot, then we return the ordered results.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) goroutines; wall-clock ≈ the slowest task (tasks run in parallel).

followUps.question: Why is writing to distinct slice indices safe without a lock?
followUps.answer: Each goroutine touches a different element, so there's no concurrent access to the same memory; only the backing array header is shared and never resized.

followUps.question: How would you add a timeout for the whole batch?
followUps.answer: Run the tasks with context.WithTimeout and select on ctx.Done() inside each task, or wait on a done channel with a time.After fallback.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Make the function that starts goroutines responsible for stopping them. Bound concurrency with worker pools or a weighted semaphore so load spikes can't spawn unlimited goroutines.
productionDeepDive.performance: Goroutines are cheap but not free; for huge numbers of short tasks, a fixed worker pool beats spawning one goroutine per task and reduces scheduler churn.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Coordinate with channels and context rather than shared mutable state. Run tests with the -race flag; prefer message passing to locks on hot paths.
productionDeepDive.reliability: A panic in a goroutine with no recover crashes the whole process — wrap long-lived worker loops with recover and restart them. Always provide a cancellation path to avoid leaks.
productionDeepDive.observability: Export runtime.NumGoroutine() as a metric and alert on monotonic growth; capture goroutine pprof profiles to locate leaks.
productionDeepDive.security: Synchronize access to shared state so races can't corrupt data or security-sensitive decisions; validate per-goroutine results before merging.

caseStudies.solution: Handle each connection in its own goroutine.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Simple and scalable, but a slow handler holds a goroutine; you still need timeouts and limits.
caseStudies.lessons: Per-request goroutines are idiomatic, but always bound downstream work and set deadlines.

caseStudies.problem: Reconcile many resources concurrently without overload.
caseStudies.solution: Bounded worker pools of goroutines consuming a work queue.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Throughput vs. resource use, tuned by worker count.
caseStudies.lessons: Bound concurrency explicitly; don't fan out unbounded goroutines under load.

keyTakeaways: A goroutine is a lightweight, runtime-scheduled concurrent function started by writing `go` before a call.
The GMP scheduler multiplexes many goroutines onto few OS threads, making high concurrency cheap (~2KB stacks).
Synchronize completion with sync.WaitGroup (Add before launch, defer Done, then Wait) — if main returns, all goroutines die with it.
The big risks are goroutine leaks, the pre-1.22 loop-variable capture bug, and unsynchronized shared state; context cancellation and the -race detector are your defenses.
